screens.title: Advanced System Monitoring with sysstat and atop
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we bring together two powerful approaches to Linux monitoring. First, sysstat collects and preserves system activity over time so you can inspect what happened yesterday or last week. Second, atop gives you an immediate and detailed view of running processes and their resource deltas, and it can also log for later replay. You will learn practical commands, logging configuration, and the investigative workflow that combines historical trend analysis with per-process forensic detail. That combination helps you find root causes for transient slowdowns. By the end of this chapter you will know how to enable logging, examine binary logs, and correlate sar trends with atop’s process-level detail to form a clear incident narrative. Ready to explore the main topics and build a reproducible diagnosis workflow?

screens.title: Why historical monitoring matters
screens.narratorSegment: Historical monitoring changes how you investigate intermittent problems. A single snapshot from top or free shows the system at one moment, but many production issues are short-lived or happen at off hours. When sysstat is configured to collect periodic samples and save them, you can rewind time and inspect the exact state at a past moment. That capability is essential for root-cause analysis of incidents that resolved themselves before you could connect. Think of historical logs as a flight recorder: sar’s binary files keep multiple metrics together so you can correlate C P U, memory, disk, and network behavior across the same interval. A concrete example is a database that briefly spikes C P U at 02:30 but then recovers. Without historical data you may never see that event. With sar -u -f and -s/-e you can pull the C P U usage for that window and check for corresponding disk wait or network anomalies. A common misconception is that averages hide problems; sar does report interval averages, so you should choose a collection interval that captures the burst scale you care about. Key takeaway: enable periodic collection, keep the files, and use them to form a timeline before you act.

keyIdea.title: Historical context matters
keyIdea.text: Saved system samples let you reconstruct incidents and correlate resource trends across subsystems.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Historical Monitoring
Definition
Periodic collection of system metrics and storage of samples for later analysis.
Why it matters
  • Reconstruct incidents after they occurred so you can diagnose root cause.
  • Correlate CPU, memory, disk and network metrics over the same time window.
  • Identify trending degradation before it becomes a production outage.
Common misconception
Averages can smooth short bursts. Pick a collection interval small enough to capture the bursts you care about.
Key Takeaway
Enable and retain periodic samples to turn transient problems into analyzable incidents.
Concrete example: Inspecting a 02:30 spike
Run sar for that day and narrow the window to the suspected interval. The example below shows the command pattern to read today’s file or a specific day file.
sar -u -f /var/log/sysstat/sa15   # CPU usage for the 15th
sar -A -f /var/log/sysstat/sa$(date +%d)   # All stats for today
How to interpret
  • Look for spikes in user or system CPU columns, or increases in iowait when CPU usage is low.
  • Cross-check disk or network stats in the same timeframe to see correlated anomalies.
  • If you see a spike, use pidstat or atop replays to identify the responsible process.

screens.title: pidstat — per-process breakdowns
screens.narratorSegment: Pidstat fills the gap between a system snapshot and process-level detail. When top or htop shows overall high C P U or heavy input and output, pidstat lets you sample each process for C P U, memory, and disk input and output metrics over a chosen interval. For example, pidstat -u 1 5 collects per-process C P U usage every second for five samples. That gives you a short time series per process to see sustained consumption versus a single spike. Use pidstat -r for memory and pidstat -d for disk input and output. If you already have a PID candidate from top, target it with pidstat -p PID so you capture only that process. A concrete exercise: after generating a short C P U or disk load, run pidstat -u 1 5 and look for a process whose C P U% is consistently high across samples. A common misunderstanding is treating a single sample as definitive; interpret the sequence to distinguish transient spikes from sustained load. Closing question: when pidstat shows a process with high input and output but low C P U, what does that suggest about the nature of the bottleneck?

keyIdea.title: Pidstat advantage
keyIdea.text: Pidstat captures per-process time series for CPU, memory and I/O so you can confirm which process sustained the load.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › pidstat
Command patterns
pidstat -u 1 5    # per-process CPU every 1s for 5 samples
pidstat -r 1 5    # memory per process
pidstat -d 1 5    # disk I/O per process
pidstat -p 1234 1 5  # stats for specific PID
When to use
After sar or top identifies a window or candidate, run pidstat to confirm which process accounted for CPU or I/O across the interval.
Example scenario
You saw a CPU spike at 03:10 in sar. Run pidstat -u 1 10 during a repeat or test load and look for a process that shows high CPU% in multiple samples. If the process uses low CPU but high write I/O, consider disk-bound behavior instead.
Misconception
A single pidstat sample may be misleading; use multiple samples to distinguish peaks from sustained usage.
Key Takeaway

Pidstat gives per-process time-series that confirm whether a process sustained the load or only produced a transient spike.

screens.title: The sysstat suite: sar, sadc, and friends
screens.narratorSegment: Sysstat is a family of utilities whose core power comes from scheduled collection and saved samples. The data collector sadc runs periodically — often via cron — to write binary sample files into a system directory. Those binary files, typically named saDD where DD is the day number, are the canonical historical record you query with sar. The sar command supports focused reports: sar -u for C P U, -r for memory, -b for block input and output, -n for network, and many more like -q for run queue statistics and -W for swap activity. There’s also sar -d for per-device block stats and sar -A for a complete dump of all collected metrics. A typical sysadmin workflow is to ensure sadc runs every ten minutes, confirm that sa files appear in /var/log/sysstat, and then use sar -f to inspect a particular day. A practical tip: sar reports interval averages, so choose your collection interval to capture the temporal resolution you need. Misinterpreting averages is a common mistake; prefer shorter intervals to capture short-lived bursts. The main operational skill is to configure and verify the periodic collection so you always have the data you need.

keyIdea.title: sadc + sar = historical record
keyIdea.text: sadc writes periodic binary samples; sar reads and reports those samples using rich option flags.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › sysstat internals
Key components
  • sadc — the periodic data collector that writes sa binary files.
  • sar — reader and reporter for saved data and live samples.
  • pidstat — per-process sampling for CPU, memory and I/O.
Useful sar flags
-u CPU, -r memory, -b block I/O, -n network, -q run queue, -W swap, -d per-device, -A all stats.
File locations & examples
/var/log/sysstat/sa15   # binary samples for day 15
sar -u -f /var/log/sysstat/sa15   # read CPU stats for that day
sar -A -f /var/log/sysstat/sa$(date +%d)   # all stats for today
Operational tip
Schedule sadc at an interval that matches the burst duration you need to capture; ten minutes is common but not universal.

screens.title: Configuring sysstat for continuous collection
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring sysstat for continuous collection is about three small steps: ensure the periodic collection job exists, verify the data collector runs, and confirm that sa files are created. On many distributions a small cron entry or systemd timer runs sadc periodically. Look for entries in /etc/cron. d/sysstat or a systemd service that starts sadc at a configured interval like ten minutes. You can force collection immediately with the sa1 helper, which lets you simulate a scheduled sample and validate that the data directory receives a new sa file. As an example workflow: check the cron or timer to confirm the schedule, run sudo /usr/lib/sysstat/sa1 to write a sample now, then list /var/log/sysstat to see the saDD file with an updated timestamp. A practical verification step is to run sar -A -f that file to ensure readable data. A frequent mistake is assuming the package alone starts logging; you must ensure the cron job or service is enabled. After configuration, monitor retention and rotate logs if disk space or retention policy requires it. The final question to consider: how often should you collect samples to balance resolution and storage?

keyIdea.title: Enable and verify
keyIdea.text: Confirm the cron or timer, force a sample with sa1, and inspect /var/log/sysstat to ensure binary logs are being written.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Configure sysstat
Checklist
  1. Check for cron or systemd timer entries in /etc/cron.d/sysstat or systemd timers.
  2. Force an immediate sample with sudo /usr/lib/sysstat/sa1.
  3. Verify sa files appear in /var/log/sysstat or /var/log/sa.
  4. Use sar -f to inspect the newly created file.
Quick verification commands
ls -l /var/log/sysstat/
sudo /usr/lib/sysstat/sa1    # force a collection
sar -A -f /var/log/sysstat/sa$(date +%d)
If files are not created, ensure the sysstat package’s collection job is enabled. Also verify file rotation/retention policies so logs are available when you need them.

screens.title: Introducing atop
screens.narratorSegment: Atop is an interactive monitor that reports multiple subsystems at once and emphasizes process deltas and input and output. Unlike top, atop shows per-process disk and network input and output directly in its main view and highlights processes that produced activity even if they have since exited. This is especially useful when short bursts finish before you can check a process table. Running atop in real time gives you C P U, MEM, DSK, NET and PRC sections together so you can correlate a high disk queue with a process showing large write activity. Another powerful feature is logging: atop can write interval logs to /var/log/atop which you can later replay with atop -r. When replaying, you can step through intervals, sort processes by C P U, memory, disk or network, and see which process was responsible at each moment. A common mistake is assuming atop replaces historical tools; instead, it complements them by delivering both immediate and replayable process-level context. The takeaway: use atop for detailed process deltas and to capture process-level input and output that other monitors miss.

keyIdea.title: Atop's strength
keyIdea.text: Atop shows process deltas, per-process disk and network I/O, and logs intervals for later replay and analysis.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › atop Overview
What atop shows
  • CPU per core and breakdown of sys, user, irq, idle and wait.
  • Memory totals and swap usage with real-time changes.
  • Disk per-device utilization, reads/writes, and queue lengths.
  • Network per-interface activity and errors.
  • Process list with CPU%, memory%, WDSK/RDSK and network R/W per process.
Atop highlights resource bottlenecks via color, and because it records deltas it can report activity from short-lived processes that have already exited. Use sort keys to focus on CPU, memory, disk or network contributors during investigation.
Run & replay
Run atop for live inspection with atop. To replay, use atop -r /var/log/atop/atop_YYYYMMDD and step through time. Use keys c, m, d, n to sort processes by different metrics during replay.

screens.title: Using atop logs to replay incidents
screens.narratorSegment: Atop logs let you replay an entire day and step through intervals to watch how resource usage evolved. After enabling atop’s logging and allowing a few intervals to be recorded, use atop -r followed by the day's file to enter replay mode. In replay you can jump forward and back in time and sort the PRC section by C P U, memory, disk or network, using the keys c, m, d, and n. A practical example: replay the log for a busy day, jump to the interval where disk queue length spiked, and then sort by d to show processes with the highest disk activity at that moment. You can then switch to m to confirm whether any of those processes were also memory-heavy. A common misconception is that replay only shows aggregates; in fact, atop’s replay shows the same per-process details as live mode. Use the replay to correlate sar trends with process-level snapshots from atop and to build a timeline that names the likely root cause process for each spike. Final reflection: how would you combine an atop replay with pidstat samples to confirm a persistent offender?

keyIdea.title: Replay for post-mortem
keyIdea.text: Use atop -r to step through recorded intervals and sort processes by resource to directly link spikes to processes.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › atop Replay
Replay commands
atop -r /var/log/atop/atop_$(date +%Y%m%d)
# In replay: use t/T to move forward/back and c/m/d/n to sort
During replay, look for the interval where a metric spikes, then sort processes to see which produced the activity. Record timestamps and process names for correlation with sar logs.
Example forensic step
  1. Replay the log and jump to the spike interval.
  2. Sort by d to surface heavy disk writers at that moment.
  3. Note PID and process name, and cross-check with sar for system-level context.

screens.title: sar vs atop: strengths and best uses
screens.narratorSegment: Both sar and atop are valuable, but they serve different investigative roles. Use sar for long-term trend analysis: it stores regular samples across many resources so you can detect patterns and narrow the time window of an incident. Use pidstat to drill down into per-process samples during a live test or reproduced load. Atop is the tool of choice when you need immediate process deltas and when you want to capture that detail for later replay. A practical example: if a customer reports a slowdown at 02:30 yesterday, start with sar -A -f to identify which subsystem spiked and at what time. If the spike suggests C P U or disk activity, replay atop logs for that day and sort processes to identify the actor. A common mistake is trying to use top or iostat alone; they give partial views and require manual correlation. The strength of the combined approach is that sar provides the when, pidstat and atop provide the who. Final question: given a brief but severe disk spike, which sequence of tools gives the fastest path to the offending process?

keyIdea.text: Sar for when, pidstat for per-process series, atop for deltas and replay; combining them speeds diagnosis.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Tool Comparison
Sar (historical)
Best for multi-resource trend analysis and narrowing the incident window using saved samples.
Use when you need to know when a problem occurred across CPU, memory, disk and network.
Atop (real-time & replay)
Best for process deltas, per-process disk/network I/O and replaying exact intervals to identify the offending process.
Use when you must attribute a spike to a specific process, including short-lived ones.
Suggested workflow
Start with sar to find the time window, use pidstat to sample processes during a reproduced event, and replay atop logs to name the culprit if it already occurred.

screens.title: Enabling atop logging and service tips
screens.narratorSegment: To get actionable atop logs, configure its logging interval and ensure the service is enabled. On Debian systems edit /etc/default/atop and on RHEL variants check /etc/sysconfig/atop to set LOGINTERVAL and LOGPATH. A reasonable starting value is a ten-minute interval to match many sysstat installations while balancing disk usage and resolution. After adjusting the file, enable and start the atop service with systemctl enable atop and systemctl start atop so logs begin recording automatically across reboots. Wait for at least one interval so an atop_YYYYMMDD file appears under /var/log/atop. If you don’t see logs, check permissions and service status. A helpful validation is to produce a short load, wait until the file is updated, and run atop -r to confirm the file contains expected intervals. Common pitfalls include forgetting to enable the service after editing configuration and setting an interval so long that short bursts are missed. The final reflection: choose an interval that captures your burst types without overwhelming storage, and align intervals between sysstat and atop when correlation is important. Enabling atop logging and service tips means set loginterval and logpath, enable the service, validate file creation, and replay to confirm log integrity.. In practical terms, log interval, path configuration, and service enablement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Start atop logging
keyIdea.text: Set LOGINTERVAL and LOGPATH, enable the service, validate file creation, and replay to confirm log integrity.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Configure atop
Edit configuration
Set LOGINTERVAL (seconds) and LOGPATH to a writable directory. Ten minutes (600 seconds) is a common starting point.
# Example setting
LOGINTERVAL=600
LOGPATH=/var/log/atop
Enable & validate
  1. sudo systemctl enable atop && sudo systemctl start atop
  2. Wait for the configured interval and check /var/log/atop for a new file.
  3. Replay with atop -r to confirm recorded intervals.

screens.title: Activity: Simulate a load and analyze logs
screens.narratorSegment: In this hands-on activity you will enable logging, produce a synthetic load, and then use sar and atop to locate the offending process. First, confirm sysstat is scheduled and force a current sample with the sa1 helper so you know files are writing correctly. Next, ensure atop logging is enabled and the service is running. Create a short C P U or disk load using tools like stress or a targeted dd write; the goal is to generate observable activity during one logging interval. Wait for the interval to complete, then pull the sar file for that day and inspect C P U, memory, and disk sections to narrow the time window. With that time window, replay the corresponding atop log and step to the interval where the metric spiked. Sort processes by the relevant metric — c for C P U, d for disk — and note process names and PIDs. Finally, run pidstat during a reproduced event to sample the process across several seconds and verify sustained behavior. A common pitfall is generating load for too short a period; ensure your load spans at least one collection interval. Reflection: how did combining sar’s timeline with atop’s process deltas reduce the time to identify the root cause?

keyIdea.title: Practice loop
keyIdea.text: Force samples, produce load, inspect sar to find the window, then replay atop to identify and confirm the offending process with pidstat.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Lab: Simulate & Analyze
Quick command checklist
sudo /usr/lib/sysstat/sa1      # force sysstat sample
sudo systemctl enable --now atop
# generate a short CPU load
stress --cpu 2 --timeout 60s &
Analyze sar
After the interval, run sar -u -f /var/log/sysstat/sa$(date +%d) to find the time of the spike. Note the timestamp for deeper examination.
Replay atop
Use atop -r /var/log/atop/atop_$(date +%Y%m%d) and jump to that timestamp. Sort by the metric to reveal the offending process.
Confirm with pidstat
Run pidstat -u -d 1 10 while reproducing the load to confirm the process keeps consuming resources across samples.
Pro tip

Align collection intervals between sysstat and atop when possible to make timeline correlation simpler.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting tips
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes slow down investigations. First, not enabling persistent logging means you have nothing to analyze after the fact. Confirm sysstat and atop services or cron jobs are active during normal operation. Second, misinterpreting sar’s averages can lead you to dismiss short bursts; choose collection intervals and inspect raw intervals rather than relying solely on daily summaries. Third, forgetting to check atop’s log path or service status can produce missing replay files; always validate by forcing a sample and checking file creation. Fourth, relying on top or iostat alone forces manual correlation and increases the chance of missing short-lived processes. Use pidstat and atop to get per-process detail. Troubleshooting tips: after changing configuration, always force a sample and replay one interval to ensure logs contain expected data. Also verify retention and rotation so logs you need are not purged. The key question: when your logs show no data for a suspected time, what verification steps do you perform first? Common mistakes and troubleshooting tips means always verify logging is active and that intervals record the resolution you need before relying on historical data.. In practical terms, avoid losing data, misreading averages, and misconfiguring services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Troubleshooting
Mistake: No logging
Verify cron/timer or systemd service, and force a sample to confirm file creation before relying on data for incident analysis.
Mistake: Misreading averages
Averages can hide short spikes. Use an appropriate collection interval and inspect consecutive samples for bursts.
Mistake: Missing replay files
Check LOGPATH, service status, and permissions if atop -r cannot find expected log files.
Key Takeaway

Validate collection and retention policies, choose intervals that capture bursts, and use pidstat and atop to attribute spikes accurately.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Remember these concise concepts as you apply what you learned. First, sysstat is the historical backbone: sadc writes periodic binary samples and sar reads them for trend analysis. Second, pidstat provides per-process time-series for C P U, memory, and input and output—useful to confirm whether a process sustained resource consumption. Third, atop is a combined real-time and replay tool that reports per-process input and output deltas and allows stepping through recorded intervals to attribute spikes to specific processes. Combining sar’s when with atop and pidstat’s who gives you a reliable investigative workflow. Also, always verify logging, pick an appropriate sampling interval, and confirm retention policies so the data you need remains available. These principles turn short-lived events into reproducible evidence and reduce guesswork when diagnosing intermittent performance issues. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we bring together two powerful approaches to Linux monitoring. First, sysstat collects and preserves system activity over time so you can inspect what happened yesterday or last week. Second, atop gives you an immediate and detailed view of running processes and their resource deltas, and it can also log for later replay. You will learn practical commands, logging configuration, and the investigative workflow that combines historical trend analysis with per-process forensic detail. For example, sar lets you pull C P U, memory, disk and network statistics for a specific day, while pidstat drills down to per-process C P U and input and output. atop shows per-process disk and network input and output in the main screen and lets you replay an entire day to step through the moments leading to a spike. That combination helps you find root causes for transient slowdowns. By the end of this chapter you will know how to enable logging, examine binary logs, and correlate sar trends with atop’s process-level detail to form a clear incident narrative. Ready to explore the main topics and build a reproducible diagnosis workflow?

By the end of this chapter you will master the capabilities of the sysstat package and use atop effectively. Objective one is to master sar, pidstat, and sadc so you can collect and interpret historical performance data. Objective two is to configure sysstat and atop for continuous logging so you can replay and analyze incidents after they happen. Objective three is to interpret atop’s multi-faceted output in real time, locating process-level input and output and network contributors to bottlenecks. Objective four is to combine sysstat’s long-term trends with atop’s detailed deltas to build a clear incident timeline and identify the root cause. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: running the right command, interpreting its numbers, configuring the service for persistence, and correlating outputs. We’ll use examples like replaying a specific day’s sar file, drilling into a process with pidstat, and stepping through an atop log to confirm which process produced a spike. These objectives prepare you to diagnose intermittent slowdowns without guesswork.

These practical objectives map directly to the demo steps you will follow. First, verify sysstat logging and force an immediate collection so you can see how sa files are created and named. Second, use sar with the -f option to read historical binary files for a specific day and use -s and -e to narrow the time window when you investigate an incident. Third, run pidstat to collect per-process C P U, memory, or input and output samples across a short interval to confirm which process produced sustained load. Fourth, enable atop logging, let it record a few intervals, and then replay a log file to step through time. Each objective includes a verification step so you confirm logging is active. Practicing these tasks teaches the full investigative loop: collect data, reproduce or wait for the event, then analyze historical logs and process-level details to reach a confident conclusion.

Historical monitoring changes how you investigate intermittent problems. A single snapshot from top or free shows the system at one moment, but many production issues are short-lived or happen at off hours. When sysstat is configured to collect periodic samples and save them, you can rewind time and inspect the exact state at a past moment. That capability is essential for root-cause analysis of incidents that resolved themselves before you could connect. Think of historical logs as a flight recorder: sar’s binary files keep multiple metrics together so you can correlate C P U, memory, disk, and network behavior across the same interval. A concrete example is a database that briefly spikes C P U at 02:30 but then recovers. Without historical data you may never see that event. With sar -u -f and -s/-e you can pull the C P U usage for that window and check for corresponding disk wait or network anomalies. A common misconception is that averages hide problems; sar does report interval averages, so you should choose a collection interval that captures the burst scale you care about. Key takeaway: enable periodic collection, keep the files, and use them to form a timeline before you act.

Pidstat fills the gap between a system snapshot and process-level detail. When top or htop shows overall high C P U or heavy input and output, pidstat lets you sample each process for C P U, memory, and disk input and output metrics over a chosen interval. For example, pidstat -u 1 5 collects per-process C P U usage every second for five samples. That gives you a short time series per process to see sustained consumption versus a single spike. Use pidstat -r for memory and pidstat -d for disk input and output. If you already have a PID candidate from top, target it with pidstat -p PID so you capture only that process. A concrete exercise: after generating a short C P U or disk load, run pidstat -u 1 5 and look for a process whose C P U% is consistently high across samples. A common misunderstanding is treating a single sample as definitive; interpret the sequence to distinguish transient spikes from sustained load. Closing question: when pidstat shows a process with high input and output but low C P U, what does that suggest about the nature of the bottleneck?

Sysstat is a family of utilities whose core power comes from scheduled collection and saved samples. The data collector sadc runs periodically — often via cron — to write binary sample files into a system directory. Those binary files, typically named saDD where DD is the day number, are the canonical historical record you query with sar. The sar command supports focused reports: sar -u for C P U, -r for memory, -b for block input and output, -n for network, and many more like -q for run queue statistics and -W for swap activity. There’s also sar -d for per-device block stats and sar -A for a complete dump of all collected metrics. A typical sysadmin workflow is to ensure sadc runs every ten minutes, confirm that sa files appear in /var/log/sysstat, and then use sar -f to inspect a particular day. A practical tip: sar reports interval averages, so choose your collection interval to capture the temporal resolution you need. Misinterpreting averages is a common mistake; prefer shorter intervals to capture short-lived bursts. The main operational skill is to configure and verify the periodic collection so you always have the data you need.

Configuring sysstat for continuous collection is about three small steps: ensure the periodic collection job exists, verify the data collector runs, and confirm that sa files are created. On many distributions a small cron entry or systemd timer runs sadc periodically. Look for entries in /etc/cron. d/sysstat or a systemd service that starts sadc at a configured interval like ten minutes. You can force collection immediately with the sa1 helper, which lets you simulate a scheduled sample and validate that the data directory receives a new sa file. As an example workflow: check the cron or timer to confirm the schedule, run sudo /usr/lib/sysstat/sa1 to write a sample now, then list /var/log/sysstat to see the saDD file with an updated timestamp. A practical verification step is to run sar -A -f that file to ensure readable data. A frequent mistake is assuming the package alone starts logging; you must ensure the cron job or service is enabled. After configuration, monitor retention and rotate logs if disk space or retention policy requires it. The final question to consider: how often should you collect samples to balance resolution and storage?

Atop is an interactive monitor that reports multiple subsystems at once and emphasizes process deltas and input and output. Unlike top, atop shows per-process disk and network input and output directly in its main view and highlights processes that produced activity even if they have since exited. This is especially useful when short bursts finish before you can check a process table. Running atop in real time gives you C P U, MEM, DSK, NET and PRC sections together so you can correlate a high disk queue with a process showing large write activity. Another powerful feature is logging: atop can write interval logs to /var/log/atop which you can later replay with atop -r. When replaying, you can step through intervals, sort processes by C P U, memory, disk or network, and see which process was responsible at each moment. A common mistake is assuming atop replaces historical tools; instead, it complements them by delivering both immediate and replayable process-level context. The takeaway: use atop for detailed process deltas and to capture process-level input and output that other monitors miss.

Atop logs let you replay an entire day and step through intervals to watch how resource usage evolved. After enabling atop’s logging and allowing a few intervals to be recorded, use atop -r followed by the day's file to enter replay mode. In replay you can jump forward and back in time and sort the PRC section by C P U, memory, disk or network, using the keys c, m, d, and n. A practical example: replay the log for a busy day, jump to the interval where disk queue length spiked, and then sort by d to show processes with the highest disk activity at that moment. You can then switch to m to confirm whether any of those processes were also memory-heavy. A common misconception is that replay only shows aggregates; in fact, atop’s replay shows the same per-process details as live mode. Use the replay to correlate sar trends with process-level snapshots from atop and to build a timeline that names the likely root cause process for each spike. Final reflection: how would you combine an atop replay with pidstat samples to confirm a persistent offender?

Both sar and atop are valuable, but they serve different investigative roles. Use sar for long-term trend analysis: it stores regular samples across many resources so you can detect patterns and narrow the time window of an incident. Use pidstat to drill down into per-process samples during a live test or reproduced load. Atop is the tool of choice when you need immediate process deltas and when you want to capture that detail for later replay. A practical example: if a customer reports a slowdown at 02:30 yesterday, start with sar -A -f to identify which subsystem spiked and at what time. If the spike suggests C P U or disk activity, replay atop logs for that day and sort processes to identify the actor. A common mistake is trying to use top or iostat alone; they give partial views and require manual correlation. The strength of the combined approach is that sar provides the when, pidstat and atop provide the who. Final question: given a brief but severe disk spike, which sequence of tools gives the fastest path to the offending process?
